subject: english
title: Grammar essentials: building a clear sentence
intro: Grammar isn't a set of arbitrary rules to trip you up — it's the shared system that lets your writing be understood exactly as you mean it. You already use most of it without thinking. This lesson names the key parts so you can spot mistakes, fix them, and write sentences that are clear and correct.

sections.heading: The building blocks (parts of speech)
body: Every word in a sentence does a job. A **noun** names a thing (dog, city, freedom). A **verb** is an action or a state of being (run, is, think). An **adjective** describes a noun (a **red** car), and an **adverb** describes a verb, often telling how (she ran **quickly**).

A few more do the connecting work: **pronouns** stand in for nouns (he, she, it, they), **prepositions** show position or relationship (in, on, under, before), and **conjunctions** join things (and, but, because). You don't need to label every word — but knowing these lets you talk about, and fix, what a sentence is doing.

sections.heading: What makes a sentence
body: A complete sentence needs two things: a **subject** (who or what the sentence is about) and a **verb** (what they do or are). 'The dog barked' is a sentence — subject *dog*, verb *barked*. 'The dog in the yard' is not a sentence, because there's no verb telling us what the dog did.

A group of words missing a subject or a verb is a **fragment**, and it usually reads as incomplete. When you check your writing, make sure each sentence has both a subject and a verb and expresses a full thought.

sections.heading: Subject–verb agreement
body: The verb has to match the subject in number. A **singular** subject takes a singular verb (The **dog runs**); a **plural** subject takes a plural verb (The **dogs run**). This trips people up when words come between the subject and the verb — the verb still matches the real subject, not the nearest noun.
In 'The **box** of old photos **is** heavy', the subject is *box* (singular), so it's *is*, not *are* — even though *photos* sits right next to the verb. Find the true subject first, then match.

example.problem: Choose the correct verb: 'The list of names (was / were) on the desk.'
steps: Find the real subject — what the sentence is about. It's 'list', not 'names'.
'List' is singular, so it needs a singular verb.
example.answer: The list of names was on the desk.

sections.heading: Punctuation that matters most
body: A few punctuation rules fix most errors. Use a **full stop** to end a complete sentence. Don't join two full sentences with only a **comma** — that's a *comma splice* ('It was late, I went home'). Instead use a full stop, a semicolon, or a comma **plus** a joining word ('It was late, **so** I went home').

The **apostrophe** does two jobs: it shows possession (the dog**'s** bowl) and marks missing letters in a contraction (do not → don**'t**). A classic mix-up is *its* (belonging to it) versus *it's* (it is) — 'its' has no apostrophe when it means belonging, just like *his* and *hers*.

practice.q: In 'She sang beautifully', what part of speech is 'beautifully'?
practice.explain: 'Beautifully' describes how she sang (the verb), which makes it an adverb. Adverbs often end in -ly.

practice.q: Which of these is a complete sentence?
options: The tall tree near the river
practice.explain: 'Birds sing' has a subject (birds) and a verb (sing) and expresses a full thought. The others are fragments — no complete idea.

practice.q: Choose the correct verb: 'The group of students ___ ready.'
practice.explain: The subject is 'group' (singular), not 'students', so it takes the singular verb 'is'.

options: It was cold, I stayed inside.
It was cold I stayed inside.
It was cold, so I stayed inside.
It was cold; so I stayed inside
practice.explain: Two full ideas joined by a comma plus the conjunction 'so' is correct. A comma alone (first option) is a comma splice.
'Its' (no apostrophe) shows belonging; 'it's' means 'it is'. The tail belongs to the dog, so 'its tail'.

summary: Words do jobs: nouns name, verbs act, adjectives describe nouns, adverbs describe verbs; pronouns, prepositions and conjunctions connect.
A complete sentence needs a subject and a verb and a full thought — otherwise it's a fragment.
Match the verb to the real subject, even when other words sit in between (the box … is).
Don't join two sentences with only a comma; and 'its' shows belonging while 'it's' means 'it is'.
